takeaways: There is more than one way to find any page in a set of pages: for example navigation, search, a site map, a table of contents or related links.
People find things in different ways. Some search, some browse menus, some scan an A to Z list. One route alone fails someone.
Pages that are a step in a process, or the result of one, are exempt. Step 3 of checkout does not need its own entry in search.
Level AA. It is about the set of pages as a whole, so plan it in the site map and information architecture, not page by page.
failures: A help center reachable only by search
Pages hidden deep in menus with no search and no links to them
Search that does not cover all the content people need
check: Pick a few deep pages and find each one in two different ways.
Check that search indexes every content type, not just products.
In the site map or IA diagram, mark which pages are exempt steps in a process.

quiz.question: A product has a main menu that reaches every page. The team wants to add search later. Does the site meet 2.4.5 today?
options: No. The menu is one way, and there needs to be a second
Yes. A complete menu is enough
Yes, as long as the menu has sub-menus
quiz.why: The rule asks for more than one way. A menu alone is one route, however complete. A site map, search or related links would add the second.

spec: Document the ways to reach each kind of page: nav, search, site map, related links.
Mark pages that are steps or results in a process, so nobody adds them to navigation by mistake.
Design the search entry point and the site map page, and note where they appear on every page.
review: If someone cannot use the menu, how else do they reach this page?
Does search actually return this page?
Is this page really a step in a process, or is that just an excuse?
tradeoff: Every extra route costs space and upkeep: search needs indexing and a site map needs maintaining. A small site can often use a simple site map page or a footer list of key pages; save full search for large sets of content.
system: Put search and a link to the site map in the shared header or footer component, so every page gets a second route for free.
pitch: People who cannot find a page assume we do not have it. A second way to find things is cheap compared to a lost customer.
